Records|Warner Bros.]] (US) | writer = [[Rod Stewart]] | producer = [[Tom Dowd]] | prev_title = [[This Old Heart of Mine (Is Weak for You)#Rod Stewart versions|This Old Heart of Mine]] | prev_year = 1976 | next_title = [[The Killing of Georgie (Part I and II)]] | next_year = 1976 | misc = {{External music video|{{YouTube|IZr6AE-u2UM|"Tonight's The Night (Gonna Be Alright)"}}}} }} "'''Tonight's the Night (Gonna Be Alright)'''" is a song written by [[Rod Stewart]], and recorded at [[Muscle Shoals Sound Studio]] in [[Sheffield, Alabama]] for his 1976 album ''[[A Night on the Town (Rod Stewart album)|A Night on the Town]]''. The song, controversial at the time of release, proved to be a massive commercial success and became his second US chart topper on the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]]. It made its debut at number 81 on 2 October 1976 and rose quickly, climbing from number eight to the top of the chart on 13 November 1976, and remained on top for eight consecutive weeks until 8 January 1977. It was the longest stay of any song during 1976, the longest run at the top for a single in the US in over eight years (since [[the Beatles]]’ "[[Hey Jude]]" in November 1968), and the longest stay at number one for Rod Stewart in his entire recording career, and the final number one of that year. The song also peaked at No. 5 in the UK, No. 1 for six weeks in Canada, No. 3 in Australia and charted well in other parts of the world. It was the number 1 song on both ''Billboard''{{'}}s [[Billboard Year-End Hot 100 singles of 1977|1977 year-end]] [[record chart|chart]] and the year-end Canadian singles chart. It became the best-selling single of 1977 in the United States. As of 2018, it is the 19th-most popular song in the history of the chart.{{cite magazine |title=The Biggest Hits of All: The Hot 100's All-Time Top 100 Songs |url=https://www.billboard.com/articles/news/hot-100-turns-60/8468142/hot-100-all-time-biggest-hits-songs-list |magazine=Billboard|access-date=12 February 2019}}

sections.heading: Background and lyrics
sections.wikitext:
According to [[Dan Peek]] of [[America (band)|America]], Stewart's inspiration for "Tonight's the Night" was America's Top 30 hit "[[Today's the Day (America song)|Today's the Day]]": Peek recalls that one evening when he and Stewart were playing together in Peek's home recording studio: "I played 'Today's the Day', the song I had been working on. Rod said that he liked it and that it gave him an idea for a song. Of course after his recording of 'Tonight's the Night' came out I laughed when I remembered what he'd said. I'm sure I probably smacked my forehead and said: 'Why didn't I think of that?'"<ref>{{cite book|title=An American Band: the America Story|last=Peak|first=Dan|year=2004 |publisher=Xulon Press|isbn=1-594679-29-0}}</ref>

The song features a French spoken part from [[Britt Ekland]] who was Stewart's [[girlfriend]] at the time.<ref name=People>{{cite news |url=http://www.people.com/people/archive/article/0,,20067446,00.html |title=Romantic Rod |first=Robert |last=Windeler |work=[[People (magazine)|People]] |date=21 February 1977 |access-date=7 February 2016}}</ref> While primarily recorded at Muscle Shoals, the final vocal was recorded at [[Caribou Ranch]] studios, where Stewart, Ekland and producer Tom Dowd spent several days. The high-altitude result was a vocal an octave higher than "sea-based" versions.  The saxophone solo is by [[Jerry Jumonville]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1989-02-03-ca-2116-story.html |title=Veteran R&B; 'Honker' Glides Into Jazz : Tenor Sax Player Strives for the Sound of '40s and '50s Greats |work=Los Angeles Times |date=3 February 1989}}</ref>

The song was originally banned by the [[BBC]] and protested by [[Jesse Jackson|Reverend Jesse Jackson]], due to its suggestive lyric: "C'mon angel, my heart's on fire/Don't deny your man's desire/You'd be a fool to stop this tide/Spread your wings and let me come inside."<ref name=rs>{{cite news |title=45 Years Ago, A Song Got Banned For The Lyrics 'Spread Your Wings And Let Me Come Inside' |url=https://rollingstoneindia.com/rsflashback-rod-stewart-tonights-the-night/ |first=Amit |last=Vaidya |work=Rolling Stone India |date=November 12, 2021 |access-date=April 26, 2023}}</ref>  Some radio stations play edits of the song, shortening the coda, as well as the whispers, because they were deemed to be too suggestive for airplay, where the songs could be banned from being played on the air.<ref name=rs></ref>

''[[Record World]]'' said, "Here Stewart's as relaxed and moving as he can be."<ref name=rw>{{cite magazine|magazine=Record World|date=September 11, 1976|page=1|accessdate=2023-03-04|title=Hits of the Week|url=https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Record-World/70s/76/RW-1976-09-11.pdf}}</ref> In 2024 ''Ultimate Classic Rock'' critic Michael Gallucci rated it as the 23rd greatest soft rock song, saying that it "[merged] impassioned soul with not-so-subtle sexed-up soft rock."<ref>{{cite web|title=Top 40 soft rock songs|author=Gallucci, Michael|accessdate=2026-09-10|publisher=Ultimate Classic Rock|date=August 14, 2024|url=https://ultimateclassicrock.com/soft-rock-songs/}}</ref>
sections.text:
According to Dan Peek of America, Stewart's inspiration for "Tonight's the Night" was America's Top 30 hit "Today's the Day": Peek recalls that one evening when he and Stewart were playing together in Peek's home recording studio: "I played 'Today's the Day', the song I had been working on. Rod said that he liked it and that it gave him an idea for a song. Of course after his recording of 'Tonight's the Night' came out I laughed when I remembered what he'd said. I'm sure I probably smacked my forehead and said: 'Why didn't I think of that?'"

The song features a French spoken part from Britt Ekland who was Stewart's girlfriend at the time. While primarily recorded at Muscle Shoals, the final vocal was recorded at Caribou Ranch studios, where Stewart, Ekland and producer Tom Dowd spent several days. The high-altitude result was a vocal an octave higher than "sea-based" versions.  The saxophone solo is by Jerry Jumonville.

The song was originally banned by the BBC and protested by Reverend Jesse Jackson, due to its suggestive lyric: "C'mon angel, my heart's on fire/Don't deny your man's desire/You'd be a fool to stop this tide/Spread your wings and let me come inside."  Some radio stations play edits of the song, shortening the coda, as well as the whispers, because they were deemed to be too suggestive for airplay, where the songs could be banned from being played on the air.

Record World said, "Here Stewart's as relaxed and moving as he can be." In 2024 Ultimate Classic Rock critic Michael Gallucci rated it as the 23rd greatest soft rock song, saying that it "[merged] impassioned soul with not-so-subtle sexed-up soft rock."

sections.heading: Certifications
Cover versions
sections.wikitext:
In 1993, Stewart recorded a live version of the song during his session for ''[[MTV Unplugged]]''. This version was included on the album ''[[Unplugged...and Seated]]''.

The song has been [[cover version|remade]] by such artists as: [[Linda Clifford]], [[Nicky Moore]], and sung by [[Kavana (singer)|Anthony Kavanagh]], [[Terry Steele]], who reached number forty-four on the R&B singles chart,<ref>{{cite book |title= Top R&B/Hip-Hop Singles: 1942–2004|last=Whitburn |first=Joel |author-link=Joel Whitburn |year=2004 |publisher=Record Research |page=550}}</ref> and [[Alison Crawford]] on ''[[Grease is the Word]]''.{{citation needed|date=May 2020}}

A version by [[Roy Head]] reached the top 30 in the USA (#28) and Canada (#17)<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.collectionscanada.gc.ca/obj/028020/f2/nlc008388.4653a.pdf| title=RPM Country 75 Singles - February 17, 1969}}</ref> Country charts in 1978.

[[Janet Jackson]] covered the song on her 1997 album ''[[The Velvet Rope]]'', although she changed the lyrics. In Jackson's cover, the lyrics imply that she and her partner are about to share a [[Ménage à trois|threesome]] with another woman. Jackson begins the song by saying, "This is just between me and you...and you." Additionally, each chorus addresses a different person, as she sings, "'Cause I love you, boy" in one and "'Cause I love you, girl" in another. "She even makes a bid for gay icon status…" wrote Neil McCormick in ''[[The Daily Telegraph]]'''s review of ''[[The Velvet Rope]]'', "climaxing (if that's the right word) with a bizarre lesbian reinterpretation of Rod Stewart's 'Tonight's the Night'."<ref>''[[The Daily Telegraph]]'', 18 October 1997</ref>

In 1993, Stewart recorded a live version of the song during his session for MTV Unplugged. This version was included on the album Unplugged...and Seated.

The song has been remade by such artists as: Linda Clifford, Nicky Moore, and sung by Anthony Kavanagh, Terry Steele, who reached number forty-four on the R&B singles chart, and Alison Crawford on Grease is the Word.{{citation needed|date=May 2020}}

A version by Roy Head reached the top 30 in the USA (#28) and Canada (#17) Country charts in 1978.

Janet Jackson covered the song on her 1997 album The Velvet Rope, although she changed the lyrics. In Jackson's cover, the lyrics imply that she and her partner are about to share a threesome with another woman. Jackson begins the song by saying, "This is just between me and you...and you." Additionally, each chorus addresses a different person, as she sings, "'Cause I love you, boy" in one and "'Cause I love you, girl" in another. "She even makes a bid for gay icon status…" wrote Neil McCormick in The Daily Telegraphs review of The Velvet Rope, "climaxing (if that's the right word) with a bizarre lesbian reinterpretation of Rod Stewart's 'Tonight's the Night'."
